title: The Witcher: Old World - I should love this game (but I don't!)
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5nA2pvB3qjA

Daniel (@dungeondive) takes a look at The Witcher: Old World — along with the Adventure Pack and the Monster Trail expansion — and finds a game that ticks nearly every box on his list without ever quite clicking.

On paper it should work: a zero-to-hero, one-and-done adventure game that plays well solo, hundreds of encounter cards, and everything fitting back into the base box with room to spare. The deck building is genuinely well implemented. Cards combo off one another by colour, there are enough opportunities to cull the chaff that you feel like you are assembling a build rather than drowning in it, and heavy attacks costing you cards next turn is a smart way to price power. The Monster Trail expansion is the highlight — hunting weakness tokens across the map to learn a creature's camouflage or vulnerabilities before committing to the fight is the closest the game gets to the video games it draws from.

The problem is cohesion. Moving between locations plays like a worker placement game with a single worker, and because there is no simple conflict resolution mechanism — no stat check, no d6 against your combat or alchemy — the Witcher you have been building barely matters until the three big monster battles. Daniel still prefers Fantasy Flight's older Witcher adventure game, but he is keeping this one in the hope that a competitive solo variant supplies the missing tension.

----

Does an adventure game need a friction mechanism in its exploration phase — a stat check, a die roll, something you can fail — to feel like an adventure? Or can pure story-and-choice encounter cards carry that weight on their own?
